tip: Μη βγαίνεις (mi vyénis) is the ongoing form: a standing rule, never go out in such heat. For just this once, Greek uses μη βγεις (mi vyis).
Έχει μεγάλη υγρασία (ékhi megháli ighrasía) – the weather 'has' humidity. Greek says έχει ζέστη (zésti), έχει ήλιο (ílio) where English says it's hot or sunny.
Χιονίζει... από το πρωί (khionízi... apó to proí) – plain present for 'has been snowing since morning': Greek keeps the present while it's still going.
Κρυώνουμε (kriónume) = we're cold – Greek has a verb for feeling cold, κρυώνω (krióno). Είμαι κρύος (íme kríos) would call you a cold person.
Θα παγώσουν (tha paghósun) = they'll freeze – θα plus the one-off form, for a single event.
Βρέχει καρεκλοπόδαρα (vrékhi kareklopódhara) – literally 'it's raining chair legs' – the Greek version of raining cats and dogs.
Έβρεχε (évrekhe) = it was raining – the ongoing past form, for something that filled the whole night.
Rain finds you in Greek: μας βρήκε η βροχή (mas vríke i vrokhí) uses βρίσκω (vrísko = to find). Bad weather, news, and trouble often 'find' people this way.
Two finished events, two one-off past forms: άνοιξα... άρχισε (ániksa... árkhise).
Θα ρίξει (tha ríksi) = it'll pour – Greek says ρίχνει βροχή (ríkhni vrokhí), the sky 'throws' rain.
Έγινα μούσκεμα (éghina múskema) = I got drenched – literally 'I became soaking'.
Φυσάει (fisái) alone means 'it's windy' – no word for wind needed. Greek weather verbs stand by themselves, like βρέχει (vrékhi) for rain.
Πρόσεχε (prósekhe) = keep watching – the ongoing command form of προσέχω (prosékho).
Κατα- makes it intense: καταγάλανος (kataghálanos) = deep blue.
Αλλάζει η ώρα (alázi i óra) = the clocks change – literally the hour 'changes'.
Προτιμάω την άνοιξη από το καλοκαίρι (protimáo tin ániksi apó to kalokéri) – you prefer spring 'from' summer: από marks the losing option, not 'to'.
Γλυκαίνει (ghlikéni) = it's turning mild – the weather 'sweetens'.
Greek doubles a word for 'gradually': σιγά σιγά (sighá sighá) = little by little, from σιγά (sighá = slowly). Same trick: λίγο λίγο (lígho lígho) = bit by bit.
Greek has no 'to' form: where English says 'started to get cold', it links two full verbs with να – άρχισε να κρυώνει (árkhise na krióni) = it started that-it-gets-cold.
Πριν πέσεις (prin pésis) = before you dive in – πριν normally takes the one-off form.
Γεμίζει κόσμο (ghemízi kósmo) – the beach fills 'people', with no word for 'with': γεμίζω (ghemízo) takes what fills it directly.
Μη μείνεις (mi mínis) = don't stay – μη plus the one-off form, for a single occasion.
Αν βρέξει (an vréksi) = if it rains – αν normally takes the one-off form for a single event.
Λόγω (lógho) = because of – the next word takes the of-form: λόγω κακοκαιρίας (lógho kakokerías).
Πότε γιορτάζεις; (póte yiortázis) asks 'when's your name day?' with just a verb – Greek packs 'to have your name day' into the single word γιορτάζεις.
Χρόνια πολλά (khrónia polá) = many happy returns – the all-purpose Greek wish.
Γιορτάζω (yiortázo) = I'm celebrating my name day – and that usually means open house. People often drop by uninvited on name days; the invitation here is a courtesy.
Τα ονομαστήρια τα γιορτάζουμε (ta onomastíria ta yiortázume) – name the thing first, then echo it with τα (ta). Greek often doubles a word moved to the front like this.
Της Παναγίας (tis Panayías), Aug 15, is the shared name day of every Μαρία (María) and Παναγιώτης (Panayótis) – one feast, thousands of celebrants.
Να (na) plus a verb turns a statement into a wish: να χαίρεσαι (na khérese) = may you enjoy. Many Greek blessings run this way – να ζήσεις (na zísis) = may you live long.
